findings.claim: Learned residual action codes, observation/goal-conditioned prediction, continuous offset, and single-pass generation.
findings.assessment: Supported by the two-stage tokenizer/predictor operations and decoded-action offset. The contrast with iterative diffusion describes action generation, not a claim that every baseline is slower.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.2-3.4, Figure 2 and Equations 4-7; p. 6, Section 4.4.

findings.claim: Competitive simulated performance and diverse behavior, with Image Kitchen and BlockPush exceptions.
findings.assessment: Supported as a broad summary: Table 2 contains both named diffusion advantages. Diversity is reported through a limited entropy proxy and qualitative rollouts; no universal entropy superiority or complete mode coverage is asserted.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 5, Tables 1-2; p. 6, Sections 4.2-4.3 and Figure 4; p. 8, Section 4.7 Results.

findings.claim: Two-phase 19/30 versus 11/30, compared with single-phase 47/50 versus 45/50.
findings.assessment: Exact aggregate counts match the modified DiffusionPolicy-T comparison. The larger sequence advantage is aggregate, not a claim of winning every individual task.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 and Table 5.

findings.claim: Onboard CPU latency 207.25 versus 5243.82 ms under fully closed-loop control.
findings.assessment: Exact CPU values and rollout protocol are supported. Controller noise is the authors' explanation for open-loop failure on this platform, not an independently isolated or universal cause.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Quantize an embedding and its residual, sum code vectors, decode, and add an offset.
findings.assessment: Supported by the actual residual quantization and output construction. The sequential encoding description does not falsely specify an autoregressive predictor configuration.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.2-3.3, Figure 2 and Equations 2-7.

findings.claim: Optional goals, single-pass prediction, competitive simulation results, and two diffusion exceptions.
findings.assessment: Supported. The performance statement allows task-dependent exceptions and does not turn the entropy report into an unqualified diversity ranking.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 4, Section 3.4; p. 5, Tables 1-2; p. 6, Sections 4.3-4.4.

findings.claim: Similar single-phase totals but larger two-phase advantage over adapted diffusion.
findings.assessment: 47/50 versus 45/50 and 19/30 versus 11/30 match Table 5. Adaptation of the diffusion baseline is preserved.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 and Table 5.

findings.claim: Closed-loop execution and fresh-action CPU cost on the low-cost robot.
findings.assessment: The protocol and 207.25/5243.82 ms CPU values match. Noise-induced receding-horizon failure is reported by the authors for this robot; the passage does not generalize it to other hardware.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Larger aggregate advantage on two-phase than single-phase trials under closed-loop execution.
findings.assessment: Supported: ten trials per task give 47/50 versus 45/50 and 19/30 versus 11/30, with modified DiffusionPolicy-T.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 and Table 5; p. 9, Practical concerns.

findings.claim: Diffusion wins the both-doors task, while VQ-BeT exhibits both closing orders.
findings.assessment: Supported: the individual counts are 6/10 versus 5/10, and both VQ-BeT orders are a reported qualitative observation, not quantified order frequencies.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Table 5 and Section 4.7 Results.

findings.claim: Final completion rates of all four longer sequences are at least three times diffusion's.
findings.assessment: Source-reporting uncertainty, not a numerical mismatch: final-stage ratios are 6/2, 3/1, 7/2, and 6/1. Joint completion of every stage is not unambiguously defined by Table 6, whose Task 4 baseline stage counts increase from 1/10 to 2/10; the authors themselves report end-of-task success.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Section 4.7 Results and Table 6.

findings.claim: CPU inference advantage matters under feedback at every step.
findings.assessment: Supported by 207.25 versus 5243.82 ms and the fully closed-loop protocol. The controller-noise explanation remains an author attribution confined to this platform.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Single-phase 47/50 versus 45/50 and two-phase 19/30 versus 11/30.
findings.assessment: Supported aggregate comparison against the adapted diffusion baseline; it does not assert an advantage in every sequence.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 and Table 5.

findings.claim: Final success rate is at least three times diffusion's on each longer task.
findings.assessment: Supported as the authors' reported final-stage success: 6/10 versus 2/10, 3/10 versus 1/10, 7/10 versus 2/10, and 6/10 versus 1/10. This does not establish superiority at every intermediate stage.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Section 4.7 Results and Table 6.

findings.claim: Both fridge/toaster closing orders are retained.
findings.assessment: Supported qualitative observation in that task. It does not imply that the diffusion baseline has only one order or that every task preserves all modes.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 Results.

findings.claim: Fully closed-loop hardware evaluation with 207.25 versus 5243.82 ms onboard CPU inference.
findings.assessment: Supported protocol and exact hardware-specific values. The open-loop noise explanation is reported by the authors, not an independently isolated mechanism.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Learn latent action tokens, predict them from history/optional goals, refine decoded actions, and generate in one pass.
findings.assessment: Supported. The contrast with direct action clustering concerns the learned latent tokenizer, not a claim that no quantization or clustering-like operation occurs.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.4 and Figure 2; p. 6, Section 4.4.

findings.claim: Competitive simulated performance and diversity, with diffusion leading on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush.
findings.assessment: Supported by the performance tables and reported diversity evidence. No precise or universal entropy advantage is asserted despite source-reporting issues in Figure 4.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 5, Tables 1-2; p. 6, Sections 4.2-4.3 and Figure 4.

findings.claim: 47/50 versus 45/50, 19/30 versus 11/30, and at least threefold final success counts on four longer tasks.
findings.assessment: The aggregate counts and final-stage ratios match the real-task tables. The wording specifies final counts rather than claiming every intermediate stage is better.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Section 4.7 and Tables 5-6.

findings.claim: RTX A4000 inference 18.06 versus 573.49 ms with all policies closed-loop.
findings.assessment: Supported GPU values and protocol. These are workstation GPU timings, not onboard CPU latency, and the passage names the GPU correctly.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Residual latent action codes plus continuous offsets provide single-pass behavior generation.
findings.assessment: Supported operations. The emphasis on action fidelity is consistent with the offset design and ablation interpretation, without asserting a fidelity guarantee.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.2-3.4 and Figure 2; pp. 6-7, Sections 4.4 and 4.6.

findings.claim: Competitive simulation performance and multiple modes, with two unconditional diffusion exceptions.
findings.assessment: Supported summary of task performance and reported diversity; neither all-task superiority nor complete training-distribution matching is claimed.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 5, Tables 1-2; p. 6, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 8, Section 4.7 Results.

findings.claim: 19/30 versus 11/30 two-task trials and at least threefold longer-task final counts.
findings.assessment: Supported by Tables 5-6 against modified DiffusionPolicy-T; similar standalone performance is 47/50 versus 45/50.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Section 4.7 and Tables 5-6.

findings.claim: Robot-specific receding-horizon failure motivates closed-loop execution; GPU latency is 18.06 versus 573.49 ms.
findings.assessment: Supported as the authors' practical report and exact workstation GPU measurement, with the platform-specific scope preserved.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Larger sequence advantage: 47/50 versus 45/50 standalone and 19/30 versus 11/30 two-task.
findings.assessment: Exact aggregate comparison is supported against modified DiffusionPolicy-T. It establishes the observed aggregate difference, not a causal effect of horizon length alone.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 and Table 5.

findings.claim: Each of four longer tasks has at least three times the baseline's final success count over ten trials.
findings.assessment: Supported final-stage counts: 6 versus 2, 3 versus 1, 7 versus 2, and 6 versus 1. Counts at earlier stages need not follow this ranking.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Table 6.

findings.claim: Both fridge/toaster orders accompany the observed sequence performance.
findings.assessment: Supported qualitative diversity report, not an isolated explanation for the aggregate success advantage.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 Results.

findings.claim: Closed-loop evaluation and 18.06/573.49 ms RTX A4000 inference.
findings.assessment: Supported protocol and exact GPU timing. Controller imprecision is the authors' explanation for this robot's receding-horizon failure.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Similar standalone totals but different two-task completion totals.
findings.assessment: Supported: 47/50 versus 45/50 and 19/30 versus 11/30. This is an aggregate association, not proof that horizon alone causes the gap.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Table 5 and Section 4.7 Results.

findings.claim: At least threefold final success counts across four longer tasks, ten trials each.
findings.assessment: Supported literally by the last reported-stage counts in Table 6; no all-stage dominance is implied.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Table 6.

findings.claim: Fully closed-loop rollout and workstation GPU inference of 18.06 versus 573.49 ms.
findings.assessment: Supported. The reported receding-horizon failure is limited to the low-cost platform, and the named GPU avoids conflating workstation and onboard CPU measurements.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section 4.7 Practical concerns and Table 7.

findings.claim: Both closing orders show diversity alongside the aggregate advantage.
findings.assessment: Supported as an accompanying qualitative observation. It does not claim diversity causes the gain or that VQ-BeT wins the both-doors task itself, where it scores 5/10 versus diffusion's 6/10.
findings.source: lee24y.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section 4.7 Results and Table 5.

findings.claim: Separate IL/RL proposals are selected with target Q in interaction and bootstrapping, greedily or through value-weighted sampling.
findings.assessment: Supported operations, including the soft variant. Alignment concerns the hybrid selection rule; online and bootstrap proposals still use the current and target RL actors respectively.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Section IV-A, Equations 1-4.

findings.claim: Separate architecture preferences and proposal-removal losses despite actor dropout.
findings.assessment: Supported in Robomimic: ResNet-18 is stronger for BC, the proposed network for RL, and Square ablations retain dropout when removing proposals. These are configuration-specific effects, not universal necessities.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 7-8, Section V-D, Figures 5-7.

findings.claim: Robomimic advantage but similar Meta-World performance to fine-tuning.
findings.assessment: Supported distinction. Meta-World disables IBRL actor dropout and uses ConvNets; Robomimic uses stronger pixel architecture and tests pixel/state settings.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 6-7, Section V-C, Figures 3-4.

findings.claim: Hang: 30 demonstrations, 30K steps, 85/65/35/15 percent success, twenty evaluations, and manual resets.
findings.assessment: All values and conditions match the real-task evaluation; the result is not an in-training exploration success rate.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Sections VI-A and VI-B, Table I.

findings.claim: Imitation supplies proposals during interaction and target computation without a BC regularizer on the RL actor.
findings.assessment: Supported central distinction from regularized fine-tuning. IBRL also initializes replay with demonstrations; the passage does not deny that additional use.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Section IV-A; pp. 5-6, Section V-B.

findings.claim: Different visual architectures, actor dropout, and complementary proposal effects.
findings.assessment: Supported by architecture comparisons and Square component ablations. The proposal-removal findings hold with dropout retained and do not claim an isolated causal explanation of every task.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 7-8, Section V-D, Figures 5-7.

findings.claim: Faster learning on Robomimic, while fine-tuning is similar on Meta-World.
findings.assessment: Supported under the paper's differing task/implementation conditions, without claiming strict superiority over RFT on the simpler benchmark.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 5-7, Sections V-A and V-C, Figures 3-4.

findings.claim: Only IBRL exceeds BC on Hang: 85 versus 65, 35, and 15 percent after 30K steps using 30 demonstrations and manual resets.
findings.assessment: Supported within the tested budget. Table I reports checkpoint evaluations rather than a guaranteed or all-task improvement over BC.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Sections VI-A and VI-B, Table I.

findings.claim: Hang checkpoint success 85/35/15 percent versus BC's 65, with 30 demonstrations and 30K RL steps.
findings.assessment: Exact values and budgets match; twenty matched-condition evaluations support a twenty-percentage-point, not twenty-percent-relative, gain over BC.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section VI-B Hang and Table I.

findings.claim: Hardware uses sparse success rewards and manual resets.
findings.assessment: Supported conditions; this is not autonomous resetting or dense-reward training.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section VI-A; pp. 9-10, Limitations and Future Work.

findings.claim: Square ablations show proposal benefits beyond actor regularization.
findings.assessment: Supported by dropout-enhanced baselines and removals with dropout retained. Dropout gains are modality-dependent: RFT improves in pixel/state, RLPD particularly in state.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 7, Section V-D, Figures 5-6.

findings.claim: Ablations establish component contributions while Hang separately documents reference-policy improvement.
findings.assessment: Supported separation of evidence: component interventions occur on simulated Square, and Hang supplies the hardware outcome. No Hang-specific causal ablation is claimed.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 7, Section V-D; p. 9, Section VI-B and Table I.

findings.claim: Hang improves from 65 to 85 percent, while RFT/RLPD achieve 35/15 percent, using 30 demonstrations and 30K steps.
findings.assessment: Supported exact values and twenty-percentage-point subtraction. Twenty matched-condition checkpoint evaluations, sparse reward, and manual training resets match the protocol.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Sections VI-A and VI-B, Table I.

findings.claim: Square proposal-removal and dropout-enhanced-baseline comparisons favor IBRL.
findings.assessment: Supported within simulated Square: removing proposals degrades performance with dropout retained, and enhanced baselines remain less sample efficient.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 7, Section V-D, Figures 5-6.

findings.claim: The Square ablations distinguish this Hang benefit from actor regularization alone.
findings.assessment: Ambiguous cross-setting causal attribution: if 'this benefit' means the preceding twenty-point Hang gain, Square ablations do not isolate its hardware cause. They support proposal contributions on Square; a general algorithm-level interpretation is possible, but no Hang proposal/dropout ablation is supplied.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 7, Section V-D, Figures 5-6; p. 9, Section VI-B Hang and Table I.

findings.claim: Separate imitation reference and higher-Q selection in both interaction and TD targets, without an imitation loss on the RL actor.
findings.assessment: Supported for greedy IBRL, used in the selected pixel Square and real Hang results. State-based experiments use the soft variant; the passage gives no specific state-result claim requiring greedy selection.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Section IV-A, Equations 1-4.

findings.claim: Separate encoders, actor dropout, shallow ViT critic, and proposal-removal effects.
findings.assessment: Supported by the described architecture and Robomimic ablations. Removing proposals with dropout retained supports contributions beyond dropout in those tested settings.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 4-5, Section IV-C; pp. 7-8, Section V-D, Figures 5-7.

findings.claim: Similar Meta-World performance to RFT; pixel Square solved within 500K with fifty demonstrations while baselines remain below sixty percent.
findings.assessment: Supported as the authors' reported solve characterization, not a claim of perfect Square success. The fifty-demonstration and pixel conditions are correctly attached.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 5, Section V-A; pp. 6-7, Section V-C and Figures 3-4.

findings.claim: Hang 85/65/35/15 percent with thirty demonstrations, 30K steps, twenty evaluations, sparse reward, and manual resets.
findings.assessment: Supported exact evaluation values and hardware conditions.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Sections VI-A and VI-B, Table I.

findings.claim: Standalone imitation proposals aid interaction and value targets without a BC constraint on the RL actor.
findings.assessment: Supported two-proposal mechanism and shared selection-rule structure. The description accommodates greedy or soft selection without claiming a true-return guarantee.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 3-4, Section IV-A, Equations 1-4.

findings.claim: Different visual encoders, actor regularization, and proposal contributions beyond dropout.
findings.assessment: Supported by the architecture design and Square ablations; the evidence is configuration-specific rather than proof of universal component necessity.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 4-5, Section IV-C; pp. 7-8, Section V-D, Figures 5-7.

findings.claim: Meta-World matches RFT; pixel Square uses fifty demonstrations and is solved within 500K with baselines below sixty percent.
findings.assessment: Supported distinctions and numerical conditions. Solved repeats the authors' characterization and does not mean a one-hundred-percent curve endpoint.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 5-7, Sections V-A and V-C, Figures 3-4.

findings.claim: Real Hang yields 85 percent versus 65/35/15 percent after 30K steps, with thirty demonstrations, twenty evaluations, and manual resets.
findings.assessment: Supported values and bounded hardware protocol, not autonomous deployment or universal improvement over imitation.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Sections VI-A and VI-B, Table I.

findings.claim: Hang improves over BC while the two RL baselines fall below it under a common 30K budget.
findings.assessment: 85/65/35/15 percent, thirty demonstrations, and twenty matched-condition evaluations are supported. BC is demonstration-trained and does not itself receive the RL interaction budget.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section VI-B Hang and Table I.

findings.claim: Drawer reaches 100 percent at 10K steps versus RFT's fifteen and RLPD's zero, using thirty demonstrations.
findings.assessment: Exact early-checkpoint values match Table I, including fifteen rather than the prose's less-than-fifteen wording. Perfect success is a finite twenty-trial observation, not a guarantee.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section VI-B Drawer and Table I.

findings.claim: These results support bounded policy improvement and interaction efficiency under sparse reward and manual resets.
findings.assessment: Supported outcome interpretation: Hang exceeds its reference and early Drawer reaches higher success at the same budget. No unobserved matched-performance efficiency percentage or isolated mechanism is invented.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF pp. 8-9, Sections VI-A and VI-B, Table I; pp. 9-10, Limitations and Future Work.

findings.claim: Hang improves by twenty percentage points over BC with 85/65/35/15 percent success.
findings.assessment: Supported exact rates and correctly expressed subtraction, with thirty demonstrations, 30K RL steps, and twenty matched-condition evaluations. It does not assign online training to the BC reference.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section VI-B Hang and Table I.

findings.claim: Drawer early checkpoint achieves 100 percent versus fifteen/zero at 10K steps with thirty demonstrations.
findings.assessment: Supported finite-trial comparison. This establishes the reported early-budget advantage without inventing the steps baselines need to attain equal performance.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 9, Section VI-B Drawer and Table I.

findings.claim: Hardware training uses sparse binary success reward and manual episode resets.
findings.assessment: Supported; reset assistance is retained and no autonomous-reset or dense-reward scope is implied.
findings.source: p056.pdf, PDF p. 8, Section VI-A; pp. 9-10, Limitations and Future Work.
